title: The oral cavity: mucosa, tongue & palate
blurb: The landmarks of the mouth, the three types of oral mucosa, the hard and soft palate, and the tongue.
question: During a soft tissue check the dentist asks you to retract the patient's tongue so they can see 'the frenum and the floor of the mouth', then notes 'hard palate and rugae normal, soft palate and uvula normal'. What and where are each of these structures?

teach.body: The oral cavity is bounded by the lips at the front, the cheeks at the sides, the palate above and the tongue and floor of the mouth below. At the back it opens into the oropharynx (throat). It has two parts. The vestibule is the horseshoe-shaped space between the lips and cheeks on the outside and the teeth and gums on the inside; the folds where it ends are the sulci. The oral cavity proper is everything inside the dental arches.

The mouth is lined by mucous membrane (oral mucosa), which differs according to the job each area does. Where chewing rubs hardest, on the gingiva and hard palate, it is tough and keratinised. Where the tissue must stretch and move, such as the cheeks, lips, floor of the mouth and soft palate, it is thinner, non-keratinised and more flexible. The top of the tongue has its own specialised covering of papillae and taste buds.

children.label: Lining
children.sub: Cheeks, lips, floor of mouth, soft palate, underside of tongue

teach.caption: Thin, non-keratinised lining mucosa absorbs drugs quickly: that is why GTN spray is given under the tongue.

teach.body: The palate forms the roof of the mouth and separates it from the nasal cavity. The front two-thirds is the hard palate: bone (the palatine processes of the maxillae and the palatine bones) covered with firm keratinised mucosa, with ridges called rugae and a small bump, the incisive papilla, just behind the upper central incisors. The back third is the soft palate: muscle with no bone, ending in the uvula. It lifts during swallowing and speech to close off the nose.

teach.h: The roof of the mouth, front to back

steps.label: Oropharynx
steps.sub: The throat, with the tonsils either side

teach.caption: Touching the soft palate or back of the tongue can trigger the gag reflex, so take care with mirrors, suction tips and impression trays.

teach.h: The tongue and the floor of the mouth
teach.body: The tongue is a muscular organ. Its top (dorsum) is covered in papillae and taste buds; its underside (ventral surface) is thin and smooth, with visible veins. It tastes, helps speech, moves food onto the teeth, shapes it into a bolus for swallowing and helps clean the mouth. Underneath, the lingual frenum ties it to the floor of the mouth; ask the patient to lift their tongue, or retract it with a mirror, to see it. The floor of the mouth and the sides and underside of the tongue are high-risk sites for oral cancer.

teach.text: Hard palate = FRONT, BONY, keratinised, with rugae. Soft palate = BACK, MUSCULAR, no bone, moves when you swallow. The order front to back is hard palate → soft palate → uvula. And don't confuse the frena: the LINGUAL frenum is under the tongue, the LABIAL frena are inside the lips.

items: Vestibule = between lips/cheeks and teeth; oral cavity proper = inside the arches.
Mucosa: masticatory (keratinised: gingiva, hard palate), lining (non-keratinised: cheeks, lips, floor, soft palate), specialised (top of tongue).
Hard palate: front, bony, rugae. Soft palate: back, muscular, no bone, ends in the uvula, involved in swallowing.
Tongue: taste, speech, chewing, swallowing; lingual frenum ties it to the floor of the mouth.
Buccal mucosa lines the cheeks; the alveolar ridge holds the tooth sockets.

summary: You can now describe the boundaries and parts of the oral cavity, name the three types of oral mucosa and where each is found, compare the hard and soft palate, describe the tongue and its papillae, and locate the landmarks you will see during a soft tissue examination.

A.q: During an examination the dentist identifies the bony structure forming the front part of the roof of the mouth. What is it?
A.why: The hard palate is the bony front two-thirds of the roof of the mouth.

whyNot.0: The soft palate is the back third and contains no bone.
whyNot.1: The uvula hangs from the back of the soft palate.
whyNot.3: The alveolar ridge holds the tooth sockets; it isn't the roof of the mouth.

A.q: The dentist asks you to retract the patient's tongue to examine the fold that attaches it to the floor of the mouth. Which structure is this?
A.why: The lingual frenum is the fold of mucosa connecting the underside of the tongue to the floor of the mouth.

whyNot.0: The labial frena attach the lips to the gum.
whyNot.2: The uvula hangs from the soft palate at the back of the mouth.
whyNot.3: The palatine tonsils sit at the sides of the throat.

A.q: A patient has a swelling on the inner lining of the cheek. Which structure is affected?
A.why: The buccal mucosa is the lining of the inside of the cheeks.

whyNot.0: Labial mucosa lines the inside of the lips.
whyNot.1: The gingiva surrounds the necks of the teeth.
whyNot.2: The soft palate is at the back of the roof of the mouth.

B.q: Moving from front to back along the roof of the mouth, which sequence is correct?
B.why: The bony hard palate is at the front, then the muscular soft palate, which ends in the uvula.

whyNot.1: The soft palate lies behind the hard palate, not in front of it.
whyNot.2: The uvula hangs from the back edge of the soft palate, so it comes last.
whyNot.3: This is the order from back to front.

B.q: A trainee asks you about the back part of the palate. Which statement is correct?
options: It is covered in keratinised rugae
It is formed by the palatine bones
It is muscular with no bony support
It is fixed and cannot move
B.why: The soft palate is muscular, contains no bone and lifts during swallowing and speech.

whyNot.0: Rugae and keratinised mucosa are features of the hard palate.
whyNot.1: The palatine bones form the back of the HARD palate.
whyNot.3: The soft palate is mobile; it lifts to close off the nose.

B.q: Which type of oral mucosa covers the hard palate and the attached gingiva?
B.why: Areas that take the friction of chewing are covered by tough, keratinised masticatory mucosa.

whyNot.0: Lining mucosa covers flexible areas such as the cheeks and floor of the mouth.
whyNot.2: Specialised mucosa is found on the top of the tongue.
whyNot.3: Ciliated respiratory lining is found in the nose and airways, not the mouth.

C.q: After an injury to the mouth, a patient says food tastes different. Which structure houses most taste buds and also helps with speech and chewing?
C.why: The tongue carries most of the taste buds and is essential for speech, chewing and swallowing.

whyNot.0: The hard palate is a bony roof; it doesn't carry the main taste buds.
whyNot.1: The buccal mucosa lines the cheeks and has no role in taste.
whyNot.2: The alveolar ridge supports the teeth.

C.q: A patient has difficulty swallowing and irritation at the back of the roof of the mouth. Which structure, which lifts during swallowing, should be checked?
C.why: The muscular soft palate lifts during swallowing to close off the nasal cavity.

whyNot.1: The hard palate is bony and fixed; it doesn't move during swallowing.
whyNot.2: The alveolar ridge holds the teeth and isn't at the back of the mouth.
whyNot.3: The labial mucosa lines the lips at the front of the mouth.

C.q: The dentist points out the bony ridge that contains the tooth sockets. What is it called?
C.why: The alveolar ridge is the bony ridge of the maxilla or mandible that holds the tooth sockets.

whyNot.0: Palatal rugae are soft-tissue ridges on the hard palate.
whyNot.1: The mylohyoid ridge is on the inner surface of the mandible, below the teeth, where a muscle attaches.
whyNot.3: The external oblique ridge runs along the outer side of the mandible, below the molars.

reteach.title: A guided tour of the mouth
reteach.question: Imagine the dentist doing a soft tissue check, moving around the mouth in a set order. What do they look at, and what is each part like?

blocks.body: Start at the front door: the lips. Step into the porch, the vestibule, and look at the labial and buccal mucosa lining the lips and cheeks; you'll see the parotid papilla opposite the upper second molar. Then the gums and alveolar ridges. Look up at the ceiling: a hard, ridged, bony front part (hard palate) and a soft, moving back part (soft palate) with the uvula hanging from it. Finally the floor: the tongue, top, sides and underside, and under it the lingual frenum and the floor of the mouth.

steps.label: Floor of mouth
steps.sub: Lift the tongue to see it

explain.body: The vestibule is the space between the lips and cheeks and the teeth and gums. The oral cavity proper is the space inside the dental arches, containing the tongue.

test.q: What is the space between the cheeks and the teeth called?
test.why: The vestibule lies between the lips and cheeks and the teeth and gums.

whyNot.0: The oral cavity proper is inside the dental arches.
whyNot.2: The oropharynx is the throat, behind the mouth.
whyNot.3: The floor of the mouth lies beneath the tongue.

explain.body: Masticatory mucosa (gingiva, hard palate) is keratinised and tough. Lining mucosa (cheeks, lips, floor of mouth, soft palate, underside of the tongue) is non-keratinised, thin and flexible. Specialised mucosa covers the top of the tongue.

test.q: GTN spray is given under the tongue because it is absorbed quickly there. Why?
test.why: The floor of the mouth and underside of the tongue have thin, non-keratinised mucosa with a rich blood supply, so drugs pass quickly into the blood.

whyNot.0: Taste buds detect flavour; they don't absorb drugs.
whyNot.1: Keratinised mucosa is thick and tough, which slows absorption; it isn't found under the tongue.
whyNot.3: Saliva doesn't activate GTN; absorption depends on the mucosa.

explain.body: Hard palate: front two-thirds, bony, keratinised, with rugae and the incisive papilla. Soft palate: back third, muscular, no bone, lifts in swallowing and speech, and ends in the uvula.

test.q: Which structure hangs from the back edge of the soft palate?
test.why: The uvula hangs down from the back edge of the soft palate.

whyNot.0: The incisive papilla is at the very front of the hard palate.
whyNot.1: Rugae are ridges on the hard palate.
whyNot.2: The lingual frenum is under the tongue.

explain.body: A muscular organ used for taste, speech, chewing and swallowing. Its top carries papillae: filiform (most numerous, no taste buds), fungiform, circumvallate and foliate (all with taste buds). The lingual frenum ties it to the floor of the mouth.

test.q: Which papillae are the most numerous on the tongue but carry no taste buds?
test.why: Filiform papillae cover most of the top of the tongue, giving its rough texture, but have no taste buds.

whyNot.2: Circumvallate papillae, in a V at the back, carry many taste buds.
whyNot.3: Foliate papillae on the sides carry taste buds.
